item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Advanced Kakuro Tactics
item.description:
The Kakuro book said “Expert.” You believed it for the first ten minutes, while the corners filled in nicely. Now you’re looking at a block in the middle of the grid where every clue has five ways to be right, your pencil marks are three deep, and the eraser has worn a soft gray patch into the paper. You’re one bad decision away from picking a digit and hoping.

You don’t need to be better at arithmetic. Expert Kakuro grids are built to resist the tools that got you through the medium ones, so you need a few more tools. There are four of them, and each one picks up where the last runs out: magic blocks give you a starting point, intersections turn candidates into digits, the 45 rule opens blocks with no starting point, and parity and forcing chains settle the corners where everything else stalls.

item.title: Mastering the 45 Rule in Kakuro
item.description:
You’ve hit a wall in an expert Kakuro. Every magic block on the page is filled in, every easy crossing is done, and a fat block of empty cells is sitting in the middle of the grid. Each clue around it has five or six workable combinations. You pencil a few, erase them, and pencil them again.

If you’ve played Killer Sudoku, your hand goes to the 45 rule. Every 3×3 box holds 1 through 9, so add up the cages, subtract from 45, and the missing cell falls out. You try it here, and you get 13 for a single cell.

item.title: Kakuro Unique Sums: The Magic of 3, 4, 16, and 17
item.description: A fresh Kakuro grid sits in front of you, every white cell empty. Your eye lands on a 27 running across five cells, so you start there. 9, 8, 6, 3, 1? 9, 7, 5, 4, 2? 8, 7, 6, 4, 2? All valid. There are eleven different digit sets that add to 27 in five cells, and nothing yet tells you which one is right. You pencil in a few, erase them, and start to wonder whether everyone else is just better at math.
